title: Cryogenic propellant transfer and tank chill-down in microgravity
bottleneck: Refueling in orbit means pumping cryogenic liquid into an empty, relatively warm tank; on contact the propellant flashes to vapor, and in microgravity a vapor film blankets the tank walls, insulating them and making chill-down slow and wasteful. Fluid slosh, ullage management, and the absence of settled gravity make metering and leak-free transfer fundamentally harder than on the ground, and each transfer event can boil off a meaningful fraction of the propellant moved.
why_it_blocks: Artemis and Starship Mars plans require many tanker flights to fill a vehicle in orbit; if transfers lose too much propellant or prove unreliable, the entire multi-launch refueling model fails.
current_state: SpaceX demonstrated intra-vehicle propellant transfer on Starship's third integrated flight in 2024, with an inter-vehicle demo planned. University research on spray-cooling and wall coatings aims to shorten chill-down. Routine operational refueling is not yet demonstrated.
